Do property auctions deliver bargains? Condo sales linked to money laundering case offer a mixed answer
article:
Four of 19 condo units linked to Singapore’s $3 billion money laundering case sold for a combined $16.28 million at SRI’s auction on Sept 23.

All four changed hands below their opening prices. But did their buyers pay less than market value?

A comparison with resale transactions at Martin Modern and Wallich Residence suggests the answer varies by unit.

One Martin Modern apartment appears to have sold at a modest discount after allowing for floor differences. The other fetched a price close to comparable sales.

At Wallich Residence, the size of the discount depends on which past sale is used for comparison and when it took place.

For this analysis, comparable transactions were adjusted by 0.4% for each floor separating them from the auction unit. This is a working assumption within the broad 0.3%–0.5% guide we have previously used. Same-stack and same-size transactions were prioritised.

These comparisons do not account for differences in condition or renovation needs. Some buyers may also be put off by a property’s links to the money laundering case.

Martin Modern: #26-10

At Martin Modern, the strongest evidence of a discount comes from unit #26-10.

Its auction price was $39,300, or 1.8%, below its last purchase price from the developer in 2020, before stamp duties and other costs.

A unit 13 floors below it, #13-10, sold for $2.1 million in August 2026. Another apartment in the same stack, #17-10, changed hands for $2.15 million in December 2025. All three have the same floor area.

Adjusting those transactions to the 26th floor produces benchmarks of about $2.209 million and $2.227 million. Their average is $2.218 million, putting the auction result about $98,000, or 4.4%, below it.

This buyer therefore appears to have secured a relatively attractive price for the higher floor, assuming comparable condition.

Martin Modern: #17-06

The other Martin Modern sale, unit #17-06, gives a different result.

Its auction price was $63,000, or 3.1%, above its last purchase price from the developer in 2020, before stamp duties and other costs.

The closest floor comparisons are #18-06, which sold for $2.058 million in October 2025, and #15-06, which fetched $2.1 million in September 2025. Adjusted to the 17th floor, they imply values of approximately $2.050 million and $2.117 million.

Their average of $2.083 million is just $3,000 above the auction result. More recent same-stack sales support a similar reading: after floor adjustments, #11-06’s July 2026 transaction implies about $2.107 million, while #13-06’s March sale implies $2.032 million.

On this evidence, #17-06 sold broadly in line with the market. Its auction sale does not show a meaningful discount or premium.

Wallich Residence: #53-01

At Wallich Residence, #53-01 initially looks like a more substantial bargain.

The same-sized #55-01, two floors above, fetched $6.03 million in May 2025. Adjusting that price down two floors gives a benchmark of $5.982 million, against which the auction unit sold about $502,000, or 8.4%, lower.

However, that transaction preceded the auction by about 16 months. A more recent sale points to a much smaller gap. In December 2025, the 1,722 sq ft #57-08 sold for $5.7 million. Applying its psf price to #53-01’s area, then adjusting down four floors, produces a benchmark of about $5.4 million. The auction price was 1.5% higher.

The different stack could account for differences in layout and view, so this is a less direct comparable. Nevertheless, it shows why the 8.4% gap should be described as a discount to a particular earlier transaction, rather than a proven discount to current market value.

Wallich Residence: #61-02

The same issue affects #61-02 at Wallich Residence.

Using #57-08’s December 2025 transaction, adjusted for area and up four floors, gives a benchmark of about $6.696 million. The auction result was only 1.4% lower.

Using #55-01’s May 2025 sale instead produces a much higher benchmark of $7.415 million after area and floor adjustments. Against that figure, the auction price was 11% lower.

Both comparisons involve smaller apartments in different stacks. Their wide spread makes it difficult to assign a precise current-market discount to #61-02. Adjusting for floor alone cannot resolve differences in layout or the price buyers are willing to pay for a larger home.

Conclusion

The four completed sales show where buyers’ offers and sellers’ acceptance levels met. They do not establish whether the auction process itself increased or reduced the price compared with other methods of sale.

The strongest evidence of a discount among those that went under the hammer, is at Martin Modern #26-10.  The other Martin Modern unit traded close to its comparable benchmark.

Wallich Residence’s results sit nearer to the more recent resale evidence than some older transactions might suggest.

For buyers, a useful question is how an auction price compares with genuinely similar homes. For sellers, competitive bidding can improve an offer, but these four sales provide no evidence of a consistent premium from choosing an auction.

title: Leasing kicks off at One Comcentre office and retail hub, with 1ha elevated park in heart of Orchard
article:
Amid keen interest from prospective tenants, leasing has officially begun for One Comcentre — billed as the first new Grade A office and retail development in the Orchard area in two decades — ahead of its targeted completion by end-2028.

The mixed-use project is the redevelopment of Singtel's former headquarters, then known as Comcentre, in Somerset.

Richard Paine, Lendlease senior advisor, development, noted that there has been "considerable unsolicited interest" in leasing space at One Comcentre.

"Over 30 tenants, mainly office tenants, have approached us. We’re looking forward to formally engaging with them in the coming months," he said during the media briefing held at the showsuite.

Singtel and Lendlease are co-developers via a 51:49 joint venture, with Lendlease set to manage the property.

Meanwhile, Singtel will be the anchor tenant, taking up about 30% of the total space including its approximately 10,000 sq ft flagship retail store. That leaves around 70% available to other tenants.

The One Comcentre showsuite is housed at TripleOne Somerset , with views of the construction site ; interactive screens showcasing the development’s technology, sustainability and employee experience; as well as virtual AI hosts and physical AI robots.

Over 1 million sq ft of offices, amenities, public spaces

When completed, One Comcentre will comprise twin 20-storey towers, injecting more than 1 million sq ft in gross floor area (GFA) of Grade A offices, retail, dining, wellness and community spaces.

Workplaces, with large office floor plates of about 25,000 to 27,000 sq ft, will make up roughly 80% of GFA. Equipped with 5G+ connectivity, the future-ready development will be able to support AI and intelligent building operations.

The other 20% of floor space will go to six storeys of amenities, including two food courts, medical suites, fitness and wellness facilities, a 400-person auditorium for corporate events, and a private members’ club.

The aim is to create a vibrant hub that brings together workplaces, lifestyle offerings and public spaces.

One Comcentre will also feature an elevated public park or ‘Botanic Ribbon’ wrapping around the buildings from levels two to four, spanning close to 1ha. Rooftop sky gardens, accessible only to occupiers, will sit at the top floor of both towers.

The development is designed by New York-based, award-winning architecture firm Kohn Pederson Fox, while the landscape design is by Field Operations, which was the project lead for the acclaimed The High Line public park in Manhattan.

"Our desire is for One Comcentre to be the new landmark in the heart of Orchard," said Gan Siok Hoon, Singtel’s group chief corporate officer, at the media briefing.

"Just like our previous Comcentre was a very iconic building, our vision for this is also for it to be the new beacon to the future, showcasing how we can bring together technology, sustainability, and human-centered design," she added.

AI-native, future-ready building centred around sustainability

One Comcentre achieves several firsts: It is Singapore’s first AI-native building powered by dedicated 5G+ connectivity, the first end-to-end carbon-neutral commercial development in the country, and the first development in Asia to obtain triple certification in sustainability and wellbeing.

"Singtel will integrate its connectivity and AI capabilities into the development from the ground up," the co-developers said in a joint release on Sept 30.

Singtel’s 5G+ network will enable network slicing, which acts as a “priority lane” or digital expressway for occupiers. This offers high-speed, low-latency and secure communications between building systems, applications and devices.

It will mean priority network performance for cloud platforms, next-generation AI applications, physical AI such as robotics, video collaboration and other business-critical operations — even during periods of peak demand.

"As Singtel is the co-developer and anchor tenant, we will always ensure that the building infrastructure and technologies stays ahead of the curve," Gan said. "Tenants can get first access to advanced technologies without having to invest in the underlying infrastructure."

In addition, tenants can tap a suite of Singtel services, including security-as-a-service and robotics-as-a-service.

As for its sustainability credentials, One Comcentre is carbon-neutral from its design and construction to operations.

The development uses low-carbon concrete and steel to lower embodied carbon, while 90% of demolished structural materials are recovered and recycled to promote circular construction.

The result is up to 30% savings on embodied carbon, equivalent to more than 7,000 cars off the roads for a year.

One Comcentre is also the first new-build large-scale development to achieve the latest BCA Green Mark Version 7 , with a Zero Energy rating. This is in addition to the WELL Version 2 Platinum Certification and, on completion, the International Living Future Institute Zero Carbon Certification.

"These credentials support our future tenants’ ESG (environmental, social and governance) ambitions, sustainability reporting and corporate targets," said Debra Ma, Lendlease director of development, Singapore, and project director for the One Comcentre project.

Tight supply in Singapore office market

The launch comes as Singapore’s Grade A office market faces its tightest supply conditions in nearly two decades, with few major developments entering the market.

The vacancy rate of core CBD Grade A offices stood at 3.3% as of 2Q2026, while the upcoming supply through to 2030 is 37% below the 10-year historical average, according to CBRE Singapore research.

Meanwhile, high-growth sectors are anchoring demand. Tech, AI, private equity, asset management and insurance firms made up 56% of office leasing demand in the first half of this year, and CBRE foresees it increasing further.

Moray Armstrong, managing director for Singapore at CBRE, said the interest from a broad range of prospective tenants in One Comcentre, even before leasing had commenced formally, reflects pent-up demand for premium, future-ready workplace solutions.

"Increasingly, we are seeing tenants expand their search beyond the traditional CBD as they look for workplaces that help attract talent, strengthen culture and support long-term growth," he continued.

"Opportunities that bring these attributes together at scale are rare, particularly within Orchard Road."

A workplace with Orchard amenities on the doorstep

The upcoming mixed-use development’s location is expected to set it apart too.

Mark Goh, Singtel’s vice president, group property, noted: "We are at the doorstep of Orchard Road. I don’t think any of the other Grade A office buildings offer an Orchard Road address and amenities."

From a lifestyle perspective, many employees would likely want to live and work in a neighbourhood with ready access to dining, retail, wellness and entertainment options. That may also encourage collaboration and innovation, added Singtel's Gan.

Armstrong of CBRE likewise pointed out that many companies’ office location strategies are determined by employee engagement as well as talent attraction and retention.

"And that's really reliant, to a large degree, on having a workplace that's amenity-rich, has experience opportunities, and is engaging and energised," Armstrong said.

Besides, One Comcentre stands out as a new-generation workplace offering within a micromarket dominated by ageing stock. Some 93% of buildings in the Orchard Road area are at least 10 years or older, CBRE Research found.

Asked about the target retail tenant mix at One Comcentre, Paine from Lendlease shared that one of the key goals is to cater to the office workers.

“Orchard Road is a fantastic shopping street in its own right, so we’re not replicating what people can access. What we will be providing is convenience and amenity for the working population in the office towers,” Paine commented.

Reviving the forgotten Tiverton Lane with F&B, placemaking

At the same time, One Comcentre is designed to integrate with the surrounding precinct and contribute to the rejuvenation of the Orchard area.

"It's a very open development and we’re going to reinstitute Tiverton Lane, which will create a thoroughfare … with retail and placemaking. So people who live around the city centre will see this as a place for lunch or a nice evening meal, and to meet people and utilise the facilities," Paine said.

Tiverton Lane, now expunged, was a small side street off Killiney Road, running through the current One Comcentre site. It used to feature shophouses, which have since been demolished.

The developers will be restoring the forgotten laneway, with hopes for it to become a bustling marketplace.

"We are bringing Tiverton Lane back as a dedicated laneway for gastro bars, cafes and restaurants as a new F&B precinct," said Ma. "It is also a thoroughfare right to Exeter Road, which will improve the accessibility of the entire Somerset precinct."

This contrasts with the old Comcentre, a 32-storey skyscraper that served as Singtel’s headquarters for more than four decades. The building, which was vacated in 2024, mainly housed the company’s corporate offices, internal facilities and its flagship retail store.

"In the past, the old Comcentre tended to be a bit more insular," Goh said. "So when we were planning the new One Comcentre, we wanted to make it more porous."

He added that the intention is to create connections through the development, linking Killiney Road to Somerset MRT Station, and provide more amenities that the community and residents in the vicinity could enjoy, such as the elevated park.

And while One Comcentre is designed for the future, the development also celebrates the history of the former site.

"There are some familiar elements from the old Comcentre, like the rooftop space frame and the phone booths, which will get a new lease of life as art pieces throughout the new development," Gan said.

title: Painting robots and heritage buildings: Wee Hur Construction's Andy Lu on tackling complex projects
article:
A water pipe more than a metre in diameter lay beneath one of Wee Hur Construction’s project sites — except it was not where the project team had expected to find it.

"We have faced projects where huge water pipes were running through our sites," Andy Lu, CEO of Wee Hur Construction, tells EdgeProp Singapore .

For that project, the location of the pipe meant the team had to change the basement’s design and also divert the pipe at their own cost.

The episode illustrates the uncertainties that can come with projects with deep basements. Underground pipes, cables and other utility lines are difficult to predict, as they may be live or abandoned, and could also be located differently from what existing records and drawings indicate.

"In construction, we are always very mindful of things that are unknown," Lu says. "We do not always know what is below ground, since we can’t see it."

Wee Hur tries to identify and resolve potential issues as early as possible, including checking existing underground services, confirming whether they are still in use and arranging diversions where needed before construction works start.

"These have to be done upfront, and the process is sometimes very tedious," Lu notes.

He says each project adds to the experience that the company can bring to subsequent jobs, even when the building type or site conditions are different.

Building and innovating through two decades of change

Lu joined Wee Hur in 2006 as an assistant project manager, and has helmed the construction arm as CEO since 2024.

Over that period, the company has expanded from a build-only contractor into a group with businesses spanning property development, property investment, fund management and purpose-built student accommodation.

Wee Hur Construction has taken on projects including private and public housing, workers' dormitories, schools, nursing homes, commercial developments, religious buildings, conservation works, as well as additions and alterations (A&A).

Lu observes that the way construction projects are planned and built has also evolved markedly across the industry over the past two decades, with far more coordination now taking place before work begins on-site.

Project teams use 3D Building Information Modelling (BIM) and digital platforms to get a clearer picture of a building and work through design and construction requirements earlier.

"With all these technologies, we are able to recreate the model of the building, and can better visualise the end-product even before we start the construction work on-site," he says.

The company is applying these tools across its current pipeline, which span a range of building types and construction requirements.

These include the Wycombe Abbey School (Singapore) in Hougang, A&A works at the historic Teochew Building along Tank Road, and the upcoming residential and commercial development on Upper Thomson Road.

These new projects range from fitting an elevated football field, competition-standard swimming pool and theatre within one school campus, to integrating new construction with an existing heritage building.

Classrooms, sports and the arts on a school campus

Slated to open fully by September 2028, the Wycombe Abbey School on Hougang Avenue 3 broke ground this January .

It is developed by Wee Hur with joint venture partners BE Education, a UK-focused admissions consultancy firm, and premier British boarding school Wycombe Abbey.

The co-educational day school, for students aged two to 18, will come with not just classrooms but also an array of facilities to support co-curricular activities such as sports, visual and performing arts, and innovation.

"This project combines a lot of different facilities, each with its own unique challenges," Lu says.

For instance, it will feature an Olympic-sized competition pool, which means the team has to adhere to prescribed World Aquatics standards and dimensions.

"There's also an elevated football field on the second storey, as well as a full on-premise kitchen and canteen serving the whole school population. These are aspects not normally seen in a typical project," he adds.

Besides, the music rooms, dance studio and theatre require acoustic treatment to prevent sound from disrupting classes and other activities.

The theatre in particular is a sizeable auditorium with a full stage and fly bars — an overhead system used to raise and lower stage equipment such as scenery and lighting during performances.

Lu says the team also has to consider circulation within the school, including how students move between different areas.

Some of the facilities, such as the library, swimming pools and sports amenities, will also be open to the public during off-peak hours when not in use by students.

With so many uses to accommodate on the site, some are stacked across different levels.

An example is the elevated, full-sized football field that will sit above the swimming pool, gym and badminton courts on the level below — a design that Lu says will "make better use of the space" available within the plot of land.

Wee Hur is bringing experience from earlier similar education-related projects to the development.

These have included building swimming pools, a sports field and basement halls for United World College of South East Asia's Dover campus, as well as an administration building and a hostel block for the Insead Asia campus in Ayer Rajah in the 2000s.

More recently, Wee Hur constructed a new 11-storey block with sports and recreational facilities at Tanglin Trust School on Portsdown Road.

Opened in early 2023, and named the Tanglin Centenary Building, the block houses a 15m climbing wall, Olympic-standard gymnastics centre, an aquatic centre with a 50m swimming pool, gym, recording studio, recital room and music rehearsal halls.

"From all these projects, we learnt the requirements and execution, and how to get them right," Lu says. "We’re using all that we've learnt to tackle challenges at the Wycombe Abbey School project as well."

Planning for multiple uses

Meanwhile, at the Upper Thomson Road mixed-use development, a basement car park will sit below a first storey containing an early childhood development centre, shops and supermarket, while residences are housed from the second storey upwards.

Wee Hur and its largest shareholder, the Goh family-controlled GSC Holdings, snagged the 262,875 sq ft site when they jointly submitted the top bid of $613.94 million in the Government Land Sale tender last October. It can yield about 595 new homes and 21,527 sq ft of commercial space.

For the group's construction arm, this means designing and planning for various typologies with diverse space requirements.

"For a residential unit, you typically have smaller spaces for the bedrooms, living room and so on, so the walls are spaced quite closely to one another. But when you go down to the supermarket, you can’t have walls every 2m," says Lu.

Each layout calls for careful planning of the building’s grid and supporting structures.

The mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems also have to be planned separately for each area, while some services are eventually combined. Wastewater discharge from various parts of the building may feed into the sewer, for example.

Clients, subcontractors and trade specialists therefore have to come on board early to "thrash out" how the design, space planning and technical systems will work together, he says.

"We have to solve very different problems at the same time and fully coordinate the requirements upfront for submission, before we can get approval to commence works on-site," Lu adds.

Giving old buildings a new lease of life

He finds conservation work especially rewarding for what can be preserved through the construction process.

"It's very meaningful because these buildings carry a lot of memory, and we are able to retain that," he says.

One of Wee Hur's ongoing A&A projects is the Teochew Building, located on the edge of River Valley. Built in 1963, the heritage property's six-storey front portion — with its distinctive Chinese roof and facade — is being conserved, while the shorter structure behind it is demolished and rebuilt.

The works include excavating a new basement carpark and reconstructing the rear portion to six storeys to match the front block.

To retain the front of the Teochew Building, Wee Hur has to protect and strengthen the existing structure, including underpinning it with piling works from within the building.

Demolishing and rebuilding the entire property would in fact be faster, easier and cheaper than conserving it.

"It's difficult, but at the end of the day, we have to make sure this heritage building is retained so that we do not lose a piece of history there," Lu notes.

Older buildings can also reveal details only after construction has started.

Original hand-sketched construction drawings may be incomplete or unavailable, while the condition and location of existing structures, pipes and other building services can become clearer after ceilings and finishes are stripped away.

Laser scanning technology helps Wee Hur capture the dimensions and existing services within such properties without relying on manual measurement and drawings.

"We can just scan it and visualise what is there very quickly," Lu shares.

Being selective with technology

Technology now plays a growing role in Wee Hur’s construction operations, although Lu is selective about which solutions the company adopts.

With a steady stream of new products entering the market, Wee Hur often meets technology vendors and solution providers to understand and keep abreast of the latest advancements.

"Sometimes it’s not easy to decide. But we stay grounded, prudent and are guided by what we actually need," Lu says.

"What problem or pain point are we trying to solve? We do not adopt for the sake of adopting. We do not want to spend money unnecessarily and do everything."

When the company identifies a potentially useful product, it trials the technology first to see whether it works as intended. Wee Hur may also provide feedback to the vendor, which Lu says can help improve the product.

Among the tools already in use are 360-degree cameras for progress tracking. A worker walks through the construction site daily with the camera to capture images, which an AI platform analyses and stitches together to give project managers and senior management a virtual view of progress.

The images can also be compared over time and against the project's BIM 3D model to check whether the completed works correspond with the design.

"This is very powerful. It enables our people to compare and take action where necessary, such as getting the subcontractor to put in more resources," Lu says.

Additionally, Wee Hur uses a cloud-based common data platform to store, communicate and share project information among developers, consultants, architects and subcontractors.

Drawings, requests for information, submissions and approvals can be handled through the platform, with each action time-stamped so that parties can easily track its status and who submitted what.

Engineers can access the same platform on tablets to refer to drawings and models and fill in digital inspection forms, which can then be signed digitally, without having to carry stacks of printed plans around.

Meanwhile, the company's AI-enabled video surveillance system flags potential safety breaches, such as if a worker standing below a load being hoisted by a tower crane, and sends the safety officer an alert and video clip for faster intervention.

In tandem, vehicle safety technology on heavy machinery, such as excavators and cranes, includes proximity sensors and cameras that warn operators and workers when people get too close.

A fatigue monitoring system also alerts operators when it detects signs of sleepiness.

Wee Hur has turned to robotics too, using it to paint the basement ceiling at the new Mount Vernon Funeral Parlour Complex project.

Lu stresses that technology and AI still need to work alongside people, as human input is needed even as more tasks are automated.

For example, with painting robots, workers still have to prepare and protect the area beforehand, operate the robot and complete any touch-ups at the areas it cannot reach.

Building capabilities for bigger, more complex projects

Looking ahead, Wee Hur is studying where technology can take its construction operations next, including reducing the industry's reliance on diesel-powered equipment.

The company is now exploring electrification as an alternative for its heavy machinery.

"All our projects are already using battery energy storage systems to cut down on diesel use and carbon emissions, and we’ve started using solar panels on the roof of the site office," Lu says.

"So the next stage is to look at whether we can use the likes of electrical excavators and electrical dump trucks."

That said, construction firms will need sufficient grid power early enough at their sites to charge the machinery, for electrification to become a viable option.

"We have surfaced these issues to the government agencies. We are working together to see how to solve this so that it makes more sense for contractors to adopt the electrification of machinery," he adds.

Strengthening Wee Hur's engineering team is another priority for Lu, who hopes a deeper talent pool will enable the contractor to take on bigger and more complex projects while maintaining its standards.

He also sees technology as one way to make construction more appealing to younger engineers, who are already accustomed to working with digital tools.

After 20 years with Wee Hur and projects spanning housing, schools, workers' accommodation and conservation, there is still one building type Lu would like to add to the construction firm's track record: a large-scale commercial development.

"We've done many types of projects, and we are always very keen on things that we have not really gone into," he says.

"Maybe it's a dream, but hopefully one day we can take on a mega commercial project."

title: SALT INVESTMENTS: Turnaround Largely Done, Says CEO — FY2027 Profitability Now in Sight
article:
Salt Investments’ FY2026 AGM on 29 Sept had a noticeably upbeat tone.

Instead of dwelling on restructuring and legacy issues, CEO Dennis Goh spent much of the meeting talking about growth, oil trading and — most importantly — profitability.

“We have largely completed” the turnaround,
and the company is now moving into a profitability phase,
he told shareholders.
The
PowerPoint deck
on the SGX website explicitly says: "Barring any unforeseen circumstances, the Group is expecting to record profits for 1H2027."
This follows from the
FY2026 annual report
released on 15 Sept, where Dennis had stated about being “very confident that FY2027 is going to be a good, profitable year for us.”

oil distribution, physical supply and fuel-bunkering business
.

Initial oil trades have already been completed, while trade-financing lines are progressively being established.
Salt’s model is straightforward: draw trade finance, purchase cargo, deliver the oil, receive payment, repay the facility and reuse it for the next transaction.

The significance is that rapid growth does not necessarily require Salt to continually issue new shares.
Its AGM presentation described the model as being funded by
“trade finance secured on cargo, not shareholder equity”
, although the speed at which the business can expand will depend heavily on the availability of such financing.

Salt has also secured its first vessel to support its physical oil and bunkering operations, reduce reliance on third-party chartered vessels and improve margins.
Management also believes owning or controlling its own vessel strengthens its credibility with customers and helps it compete for contracts.

The proposed

is intended to digitalise transactions and improve productivity and financing access across the maritime supply chain.
Dennis says much of the maritime SME supply chain is still surprisingly manual — information moving through WhatsApp, photos, and standalone accounting/CRM systems. The platform is intended to connect these fragmented steps digitally.

Salt has secured a technology licence with worldwide maritime exclusivity.
The platform is still under development, with feasibility work and a technology consortium being progressed.
In the annual report, the CEO says Salt is in “active discussions with several technology strategic partners to form a consortium”.

Goh stressed that Salt's existing operating businesses will become the platform's first users.

What about share dilution?

There was also a clarification during the Q&A.

Dennis said Salt now has less need to pursue acquisitions, as its existing businesses can increasingly be grown organically.

title: Get Smart: I’ll Wait For The Market To Fall Before I Buy
article:
“I’ll wait for the market to fall before I buy.”
I have heard some version of this countless times over the years.
And on the surface, it sounds perfectly sensible.
Why buy when stocks are expensive if you can wait for a better price?
Well, on 15 September 2026 (Tuesday), investors got their better price.
The
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) fell 79.38 points, or 1.4%, in a single day, closing at 5,638.64.
Just a day earlier, it had closed at 5,718.02.
So let me ask you a question.
Did you buy?
There was your lower price
Imagine you had S$10,000 sitting in cash on Monday.
You looked at the market and decided:
“Too expensive. I’ll wait for a pullback.”
Twenty-four hours later, the STI was almost 80 points lower.
There was your pullback.
There was your cheaper price.
Yet I suspect many investors would have found it much harder to press the buy button on Tuesday than they imagined.
Because once prices start falling, a different set of questions takes over.
What if the market falls another 100 points tomorrow?
What if this is the start of something bigger?
Maybe I should wait and see.
Perhaps it will be even cheaper next week.
And just like that, the goalposts move.
We want lower prices. But we also want certainty.
That is one of the strange things about investing.
When share prices are rising, we wish we had bought earlier.
We tell ourselves that if only prices came down a little, we would happily buy.
Then prices actually fall.
And suddenly, what we really want is not just a lower price.
We want a lower price together with reassurance that it will not fall further.
Unfortunately, markets do not usually give us both.
Lower prices rarely arrive with a note saying:
Don’t worry. Everything is fine. This is definitely a good time to buy.
Usually, they arrive together with a reason to feel nervous.
On that Tuesday, weakness across Asian markets came amid concerns over the pace of artificial intelligence development.
In Singapore, losers heavily outnumbered gainers, and all three local banks ended the day lower.
In other words, there was a reason investors felt uncomfortable.
There almost always is.
So should you have bought on Tuesday?
Here is where things get tricky.
I am not saying Tuesday was “the bottom”.
Nobody knew that.
And nobody knew whether the market would fall another 1%, 5% or 20%.
That is not the lesson.
The lesson is this:
If your plan is to wait until lower prices also feel comfortable, you may end up waiting a very long time.
By Friday, 18 September, the STI had recovered part of Tuesday’s decline.
That does not prove Tuesday was some wonderful buying opportunity. It simply shows how quickly the situation can change.
At the start of the week, the market may have looked too expensive to buy. Once prices fell, the uncertainty made buying feel uncomfortable for a different reason. And when the market recovered some ground, the hesitation simply shifted again.
That is the difficulty with waiting for the “right” moment. The reason for not buying can change faster than the market itself.
Decide before the scary day arrives
This is why I think investors should spend less time trying to predict exactly when the next correction will happen.
Instead, decide what you will do when it does.
Suppose you have S$10,000 to invest.
Maybe you do not need to put all S$10,000 into the market at once.
You could invest part of it today.
Keep some aside.
And if attractive companies become cheaper, you already know what you are prepared to do.
The exact method matters less than having a plan.
Because making calm decisions is easy when everything is calm.
The real test comes when the market falls and every headline gives you another reason to wait.
Get Smart: What will you actually do?
There will be bigger declines than last Tuesday’s.
Much bigger ones.
Some will recover quickly.
Others will not.
We will not know which is which beforehand.
So perhaps the question is not:
“When will the market give me a good opportunity to buy?”
A better question is:
“What will I actually do when it does?”
Because saying you want lower prices is easy.
Buying when lower prices finally arrive is much harder.

title: Unlocking CICT’s Growth Engine: From AEIs to a S$1.1B Hougang Expansion
article:
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT, is reshaping its portfolio.
Paragon, a freehold retail and medical asset on Orchard Road, joined the
REIT
on 1 July 2026.
Asia Square Tower 2 has left the REIT’s portfolio.
Further down the line, CICT’s S$1.1 billion commercial development at Hougang Central could add another major source of income.
How did CICT fare in the first half of 2026?
Two engines drove CICT’s distribution growth in the first half of 2026 (1H 2026): full ownership of CapitaSpring and Gallileo’s handover to the European Central Bank.
Gross revenue rose 7.5% year on year to S$846.8 million.
Net property income (NPI) grew 8.7% to S$630.5 million.
Distributable income climbed 13.3% to S$466.7 million.
Distribution per unit
(DPU) increased 7.1% to S$0.0602 for 1H 2026.
Retail was the softer side.
Retail gross revenue fell 3.9% and retail NPI slipped 3.7%, largely because CICT divested Bukit Panjang Plaza in February 2026.
Tenant sales per square foot grew 1.6% and shopper traffic rose 2.4%.
Meanwhile, office rental reversion reached 6.5% in 1H 2026, up from 4.8% a year earlier.
Retail reversion eased to 4% from 7.7%.
How does the Paragon and Asia Square Tower 2 swap work?
CICT completed its Paragon acquisition on 1 July 2026.
The deal carries an agreed property value of S$3.9 billion and an overall net yield of 3.9%.
Paragon starts contributing to CICT’s income from the third quarter of 2026 (3Q 2026).
Asia Square Tower 2 headed the other way.
The divestment was completed on 17 September 2026 at an exit yield of 3%.
The sale is expected to bring in about S$2.45 billion of net proceeds.
What about debt?
CICT’s aggregate leverage stood at 37.4% on 30 June 2026.
The cost of debt fell to 2.9% from 3.4% a year ago.
Interest cover
rose to 3.9 times from 3.3 times.
Fixed-rate borrowings made up 78% of total debt, down from 81%.
Which asset enhancement projects come next?
CICT has five asset enhancement initiatives (AEIs) lined up through to 2028.
Tampines Mall comes first.
The mall’s AEI completes in 3Q 2026 at a cost of about S$24 million, with a targeted return on investment (ROI) of about 7%.
Next, CICT expects its Raffles City Tower upgrading to finish in 4Q 2026.
Lot One Shoppers’ Mall follows in 1Q 2027, with about S$37 million of capital expenditure and a targeted ROI above 7%.
Two projects are due to start in 3Q 2026.
Capital Tower’s AEI costs about S$25 million and should be completed in 4Q 2027.
The second is also the biggest AEI.
It covers Plaza Singapura and The Atrium@Orchard.
CICT plans to spend about S$160 million there for a targeted ROI of 6% to 7%, with completion in 4Q 2028.
What could Hougang Central add?
Hougang Central’s commercial component will offer about 300,000 square feet of net lettable area.
CICT puts the development cost at about S$1.1 billion.
Based on the valuer’s estimated net income, the yield on cost should exceed 5%.
The project sits in the design and planning stage.
Construction should begin in 2027, subject to planning approvals, with completion in 2030 or 2031.
Management expects no DPU impact during the development period.
Once complete, Hougang Central could give CICT’s DPU another major boost.
What risks should unitholders watch?
Paragon’s lease expiries stand out.
Retail leases making up 30.6% of Paragon’s gross rental income expire in 2027.
That is a large slug of space to re-let in a single year.
Those renewals will largely decide whether Paragon grows income beyond the 1.7% accretion that management has modelled.
The Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link poses a second risk for retail.
Its impact is anyone’s guess, but investors cannot assume there will be none, especially for malls in the west of Singapore.
Get Smart: Follow the DPU, not the deals
Asset swaps and AEIs make big headlines.
For unitholders, the real test is whether the REIT can lift its DPU over time.
With CICT, watch where aggregate leverage settles now that the Asia Square Tower 2 sale is complete.
Then track the rents Paragon secures as its 2027 leases come up for renewal.
If both head in the right direction, the AEI pipeline and Hougang Central give CICT a path to growing DPU into the next decade.

title: Temasek-backed Mapletree evaluates India office REIT listing — Bloomberg
article:
(Sept 30): Mapletree Investments Pte Ltd is evaluating a plan to list part of its India office portfolio through a real estate investment trust as it seeks to tap growing investor appetite for commercial properties, people familiar with the matter said.

The unit of Singapore state investor Temasek Holdings Pte Ltd has held talks with banks to put four of its office parks into a REIT, according to the people, who asked not to be identified as the discussions are private. Mapletree and Canadian pension fund Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec own 40% stakes in the buildings. Temasek picked up a 20% stake last year in the properties across Mumbai, Chennai, Pune and Bengalaru.

The new trust could raise as much as $600 million by selling shares at a valuation of about $2.5 billion, one of the people said. Discussions are preliminary and investors are still drawing up the exact deal contours, but are targeting a mid-to-late-2027 listing in Mumbai, the people said.

Demand for office space is surging across the country as global and local firms draw up expansion plans for their India strategy. A September report from CBRE Group Inc said that the bulk of office tenants plan to expand their India footprint over the next two years. Despite concerns that artificial intelligence may reduce the need for office space, investor appetite for REITS has surged. Bagmane Prime Office REIT raised US$360 million ($459.9 million) through an India listing in May.

See also: Mapletree Industrial Trust to divest 3255 Neil Armstrong Boulevard at US$9.8 mil, 10% below independent valuation

Several banks such as Citigroup Inc and HSBC Holdings plc are hunting for space in Mumbai to accommodate staff. Vacancies across the top eight cities in India continue to edge lower, according to an August report by Cushman & Wakefield Ltd.

title: Canada has ‘backup plans’ in case Trump bans diesel exports
article:
(Sept 30): Canada’s energy minister said the country has contingency plans for disruptions to diesel supply, including a possible US ban on exports of the fuel.

Because Canada is a net exporter of diesel, “if push came to shove, we can deal with that,” Tim Hodgson said in an interview in Vancouver. The nation had been exempted from US energy export bans in the past because the two countries’ petroleum industries “are so integrated,” he said.

“I would say keep calm and carry on,” he said. “At the same time, we would always be running scenarios, and what-ifs, and planning, and have backup plans for those sorts of scenarios.”

Diesel prices have soared as energy supplies struggle to get through the Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran War. They have risen further following Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries that led the Kremlin to halt overseas sales of the fuel. US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that he was still “very seriously” looking at a ban to curb high prices in the US.

Hodgson voiced his support for the perspective of US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who said earlier this month that such a restriction would not work. That echoed comments by the European Union’s Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen.

“When you talk to the people who are closest to the issue in the US, like Secretary Wright, they’ve got a perspective that we would share, that it wouldn’t be helpful,” Hodgson said.

See also: Toyota sales fall for seventh straight month on China slump

Although Canada sees high prices at the pump, it’s not experiencing shortages as a result of disruption, which have already led to demand-side measures such as factory closures in other countries, the minister said.

Hodgson said he hopes to oversee a huge expansion in Canada’s energy industry and exports. He was speaking after the announcement that the country’s largest liquefied natural gas export facility will double its capacity to ship more to Asian buyers.

He said Prime Minister Mark Carney’s strategy to become an “energy superpower” and trusted partner has been reinforced by the amount of supply disruption and destruction resulting from global conflicts. “The pace of inquiry from potential buyers around the world is only accelerating,” Hodgson said. “It just tilts people more towards Canada.”

See also: Goldman's John Waldron edges closer to succeeding Solomon as CEO

Earlier this month, Carney held an investment summit in Toronto at which he outlined an ambition to unlock C$500 billion (US$352 billion) of private investment in the coming years.

Hodgson said deals in energy and critical minerals were discussed at the conference that could be a comparable scale to the C$33 billion LNG Canada expansion investment announced on Tuesday.

Referring to the amount of capital committed by LNG Canada’s investors, he added: “Well, these guys have done C$70 billion so far, and I would be surprised if they didn’t do more.”

title: South Korea tax revenue to hit fresh record on global chip boom
article:
(Sept 30): South Korea expects its national tax revenue to soar to a record high this year, underscoring the scale of a semiconductor-driven windfall underpinning President Lee Jae Myung’s ambitious investment agenda.

Tax receipts are forecast to reach 478.6 trillion won (US$353 billion or $450 billion) in 2026, up 28% from last year, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy. That would exceed the estimate used in this year’s supplementary budget by 63.2 trillion won, or 15.2%, as chip profits, special dividends and stock trading generate more revenue than anticipated.

The projections would put annual collections above 400 trillion for the first time, and roughly 21% higher than the previous record set in 2022. The 104.7 trillion won increase from last year illustrates how the artificial intelligence boom is reshaping South Korea’s state finances as well as its export-driven economy.

The windfall is central to Lee’s plans to channel the chip boom into longer-term investment. The government has proposed raising spending by a record 12.8% to 820.9 trillion won next year, with funding for AI, chip infrastructure and programmes aimed at spreading the benefits of growth.

Under that proposal, the so-called new Future Response Fund would receive 162.3 trillion won, largely reflecting tax revenue expected to exceed its long-term trend. Of that, 45.4 trillion won would finance programmes already included in next year’s spending plan, while the rest would help reduce new bond issuance and build reserves for future needs.

See also: Australia raises key rate to 15-year high to cool inflation

The latest revision shows how quickly chip earnings have outpaced the government’s assumptions. The impact extends beyond corporate taxes. Bigger bonuses in the semiconductor and financial sectors are boosting income-tax receipts, while Samsung Electronic Co’s announced plan to pay 30 trillion won in third-quarter cash dividends is adding to dividend-tax revenue.

Stronger stock trading has increased tax receipts from securities transactions, while recovering private consumption and rising imports have supported value-added tax receipts, the ministry said. Increased home transactions are also boosting capital gains tax revenue.

The surge also highlights the importance of semiconductor earnings to the government’s fiscal ambitions. Its proposed expansion of spending and investment rests in part on an exceptional increase in tax receipts from an industry prone to sharp swings in profitability.

title: Radiant World deepens job cuts after founder loses control of firm — Bloomberg
article:
(Sept 30): Radiant World is cutting staff beyond its core iron-ore business after a Singapore court last week took control of the troubled commodity trader away from its founder.

The latest reductions include staff working in operations and execution for base metals, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing private information. Those functions had been relatively insulated from previous cuts, which were heavily focused on its iron-ore unit.

Radiant’s base-metals trading business, focused on refined copper and primary aluminium, operated largely independently from its iron-ore division. A number of employees in the unit had remained at Radiant even as the company shed traders and operations staff elsewhere in recent months.

The iron-ore business has been at the centre of allegations that Radiant provided falsified documents to secure hundreds of millions of dollars in financing.

A spokesperson for Radiant World wasn’t immediately able to comment on the latest job cuts.

Radiant has been under mounting pressure since Bloomberg reported in late July that top commodity traders including Glencore plc had moved to cut ties with the company amid concerns it had provided falsified records of iron-ore trades to lenders. Radiant has denied wrongdoing and said it conducts its business to the highest commercial and legal standards.

See also: Copper edges higher after Chile mine union rejects pay offer

A Singapore court appointed KPMG restructuring executives to take charge of the trader’s key operation unit in the country on Sept 24, wresting control away from founder Pinkesh Nahar at the request of creditor Mizuho Bank Ltd.

Mizuho sought judicial management after suing Radiant over US$97.3 million ($124.35 million) in receivables purportedly arising from iron ore sales to Glencore International AG. The bank said in a court filing that it had strong reasons to believe it was the victim of fraud perpetrated by Radiant.

The latest reductions follow at least two earlier rounds of job cuts since July. Radiant had already lost almost half its iron ore traders in China and Singapore, while there had also been departures from its London and Geneva offices, Bloomberg reported earlier this month.

See also: Demand boost for US crops still unclear after China tariff cuts

The company had also more than halved its iron-ore operations staff in China, while traders in London and Geneva had largely closed out their positions and ceased trading, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg at the time.

title: Asian stocks rise, bonds steady before PCE data
article:
(Sept 30): Asian stocks gained for the first time in three sessions as easing oil-market concerns helped stem a bruising bond sell-off ahead of a crucial US inflation reading. The dollar was set for its best month since June.

The MSCI Asia Pacific Index advanced 0.4%, led by technology companies after a key gauge of US semiconductor shares rose. US equity-index futures also edged up.

Bonds remained in focus after yields on the longest-dated Treasuries reached their highest since 2002 in the New York session. The benchmark 10-year steadied in early Asian trading following losses earlier this week, when a rally in oil prompted traders to price in further interest-rate hikes by the Federal Reserve (Fed).

Helping sentiment was Tuesday’s decline in oil, with global benchmark Brent falling 2.6% to settle below US$103 a barrel. The drop came as Saudi Arabia was said to have restored about half the capacity of its East-West pipeline following drone attacks. The Trump administration also ordered another release from emergency reserves as US-Iran talks remained deadlocked. Prices rebounded 0.3% on Wednesday.

Oil prices and US-Iran tensions remain key sources of uncertainty, with markets looking for clearer signs of progress in negotiations after conflicting signals in recent days. Global bond yields have climbed to multi-year highs as elevated energy costs threaten to keep inflation persistent and reinforce expectations for further Fed interest-rate hikes.

“The sell-off in bonds can stop for one of the following reasons: a quick resolution of the US-Iran conflict, a material fall in stock prices driven by a slowdown in hard economic data, or lower earnings and forward guidance,” said Arjun Vij, a portfolio manager at JPMorgan Asset Management.

See also: Treasuries stabilise after sell-off, stocks slip

Yields on the Treasury’s longest-dated bond rose for a sixth straight day on Tuesday as investors demanded greater compensation to hold bonds amid concerns about persistent inflation, government spending and a surge in corporate borrowing to finance the artificial-intelligence buildout.

Traders are ramping up bets that Treasury yields will keep climbing from their current roughly two-decade highs, raising the risk of an abrupt unwind of those positions on any sign of a marked economic cooling.

Money markets are pricing a series of rate hikes over the next year.

See also: Bonds drop with stocks as Iran tensions boost oil

Elsewhere, China unveiled mortgage subsidies and changes to bank lending policies, stepping up efforts to support an economy losing momentum.

In other corners of the market, gold was a touch weaker at US$4,175 an ounce.

A Bloomberg gauge of the dollar steadied on Wednesday, wrapping up its best month since June as the Fed’s renewed focus on taming inflation pushed rate expectations and US bond yields higher.

The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index has risen 1.9% in September, touching the highest level in two months.

Meanwhile, New York Fed President John Williams said another interest-rate hike “late this year” may be appropriate to help bring inflation down, though he added there was no urgency to act after the central bank raised rates earlier this month.

Other policymakers also kept the prospect of further hikes in focus. Fed governor Michael Barr repeated his warning that more increases may be needed to slow inflation, while Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee said the central bank must respond to supply shocks.

Alongside signals from Fed officials, investors assessed data showing US consumer confidence fell in September to its lowest since 2014 as views of the economy and labour market deteriorated. Job openings declined in August, pointing to softer hiring demand, while layoffs remained subdued.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The next data point is Wednesday’s Bureau of Economic Analysis’ personal consumption expenditures reading, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. August’s personal income and outlays report should show an acceleration in monthly headline and core inflation, according to Bloomberg Economics.

Upside surprises would reinforce the Fed’s hawkish stance and support the case for further tightening, wrote Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade. Softer numbers, however, could raise questions about the need for a follow-up rate hike in October and potentially take some of the steam out of the recent rise in Treasury yields.

“Between the oil price, bond yields and key US inflation and jobs data, there is plenty of things to keep an eye on for the rest of the week,” Waterer wrote.
• OpenAI aims to raise at least US$30 billion ($38.34 billion) from investors in a new round of funding, according to people familiar with the matter, after the AI startup pushed back its plans for an initial public offering.
• Apple Inc chief executive officer John Ternus is moving to overhaul the iPhone maker in an effort to accelerate product development, broaden its range of devices and create a leaner organisation with a greater focus on engineering.
• Paramount Skydance Corp is promising to cut US$6 billion in costs within three years as it looks to lock in lenders for its blockbuster Warner Bros Discovery Inc acquisition.
• Anthropic PBC warned that its technology poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” and mapped out plans to spend hundreds of billions of dollars in its prospectus, Reuters reported.

Some of the main moves in markets:
• The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index was little changed
• The euro was little changed at US$1.1336
• The Japanese yen rose 0.1% to 157.11 per dollar
• The offshore yuan was little changed at 6.7073 per dollar
• The Australian dollar was little changed at US$0.6989
• The yield on 10-year Treasuries was little changed at 5.24%

title: Oil holds loss as Middle East exports seen near pre-war level
article:
(Sept 30): Oil steadied after its biggest drop in more than a week on signs supply from the Middle East has risen to near pre-war levels as Saudi Arabia resumed flows through a pipeline that avoids the Strait of Hormuz.

West Texas Intermediate slipped toward US$89 a barrel after dropping 3.5% in the previous session, while Brent settled near US$103. Crude exports from the Middle East have rebounded to 17.5 million barrels a day, or 98% of pre-war levels, JPMorgan analysts led by Natasha Kaneva said in a note.

That comes as Saudi Arabia restored flows through its East-West pipeline to at least 3.5 million barrels a day, about half its capacity, according to people familiar with the matter. However, supply of products from the Middle East, such as diesel and gasoline, are at just 58% of pre-war levels, JPMorgan said.

Meanwhile, the US will tap more oil from emergency reserves, offering further supply relief as the government grapples with surging fuel prices less than two months before the midterm elections. The release of as much as 40 million barrels will be the last of the nation’s 172 million-barrel contribution to a coordinated drawdown of global reserves since the war began.

Crude is still headed for a third monthly gain on escalating US-Iran tensions, the earlier disruptions to the Saudi bypass route and potential diesel export curbs by Washington. Brent is up almost 70% this year, after more than seven months of conflict in the Middle East.

Elsewhere, key Opec+ members are likely to stick with a plan to hold crude production quotas steady for next month when they meet this weekend, according to two delegates. The group, led by Saudi Arabia and Russia, will probably ratify their existing roadmap to keep targets unchanged in November.

See also: Asia may weather tight global diesel market better than Europe — Bloomberg analysis

title: US stocks fall as long-term yields hit 24-year high
article:
(Sept 30): Stocks joined bonds lower as a drop in oil prices did little to allay Wall Street’s concerns that still-elevated energy costs could fuel inflation and spur Federal Reserve (Fed) rate hikes.

Those worries sent Treasury 30-year yields to the highest level since 2002. Most companies in the S&P 500 fell, with the gauge posting back-to-back losses. The dollar rose. The euro hit its weakest in 16 months. Brent crude dropped below US$103 a barrel as the Trump administration ordered another release of oil from emergency reserves amid a stalemate in US-Iran talks.

“The conflict in the Middle East and the implications for forward inflation remain the primary macro narrative and are likely to dictate price action in US rates for the foreseeable future,” said Ian Lyngen at BMO Capital Markets.

Investors are demanding greater compensation to hold bonds as concerns about persistent inflation, government spending and surging corporate borrowing to finance the artificial-intelligence buildout intensify. Against this backdrop, money markets are pricing a series of rate hikes over the next year.

Fed Bank of New York President John Williams said one more rate increase this year may be appropriate to help contain inflation, but added there’s no urgency to act following the central bank’s decision to lift rates this month. Following his remarks, traders dialed back their bets on an October hike.

“We read this as most consistent with skipping October and hiking in December,” said Krishna Guha at Evercore.

See also: US stocks waver as oil rally triggers bond volatility

Meantime, Fed Governor Michael Barr on Tuesday repeated a warning that further rate increases will likely be needed to slow inflation.

In economic news, US job openings fell to a five-month low, suggesting employers grew more cautious about expanding their workforces toward the end of the summer, while layoffs remained subdued. Consumer confidence dropped to the lowest level since 2014.

The latest labor-market data reinforces the “low-hire, low-fire” backdrop that has taken hold, according to Bret Kenwell at eToro. On the consumer-confidence front, he says the disappointing headline figure should not come as a surprise.

See also: US stocks fall as inflation jitters boost bond yields

“Sentiment now sits at multi-year lows as persistent inflation and higher costs weigh on households,” Kenwell noted. “The question becomes whether we’ll see this materialise into weaker consumer spending — a question that earnings season will help answer.”
